Exploring Human Health Data with ggplot2 and dplyr

Alex Gresham

2026-06-10

Introduction

In this exercise you will work with a dataset of 200 human samples containing physical measurements and clinical lab values. You will practice:

  • Reading tabular data into R
  • Manipulating data with dplyr (filter, select, mutate, group_by, summarize)
  • Visualizing data with ggplot2

The dataset (human_health_data.tsv) contains the following columns:

Column Description
sample_id Unique sample identifier
sex Biological sex (Male / Female)
height_cm Height in centimetres
weight_kg Weight in kilograms
hair_color Hair color
eye_color Eye color
blood_glucose_mgdl Fasting blood glucose (mg/dL)
LDL_mgdl LDL cholesterol (mg/dL)

Part 1 — Loading the data

1.1 Load the tidyverse package and read human_health_data.tsv into a tibble called health. Use read_tsv(). Print the first few rows with head().

# Your code here
library(tidyverse)

health <- read_tsv("human_health_data.tsv")

head(health)

1.2 Use glimpse() to get an overview of the data types in health.

# Your code here
glimpse(health)
Rows: 200
Columns: 8
$ sample_id          <chr> "S001", "S002", "S003", "S004", "S005", "S006", "S007", "S008",…
$ sex                <chr> "Male", "Male", "Female", "Female", "Female", "Female", "Male",…
$ height_cm          <dbl> 182.5, 175.5, 164.5, 162.3, 154.3, 167.0, 179.9, 165.9, 171.9, …
$ weight_kg          <dbl> 83.5, 80.4, 82.4, 75.5, 55.9, 54.6, 47.5, 76.8, 80.1, 60.8, 77.…
$ hair_color         <chr> "Blonde", "Brown", "Blonde", "Brown", "Gray", "Blonde", "Brown"…
$ eye_color          <chr> "Hazel", "Blue", "Blue", "Brown", "Brown", "Brown", "Blue", "Br…
$ blood_glucose_mgdl <dbl> 95.7, 100.5, 97.3, 95.8, 89.3, 98.2, 98.9, 85.7, 84.8, 90.3, 75…
$ LDL_mgdl           <dbl> 157.1, 127.6, 117.4, 107.4, 85.1, 88.5, 71.0, 84.4, 122.7, 96.4…

Part 2 — Selecting and filtering (select, filter)

2.1 Create a new tibble called clinical that contains only the columns sample_id, sex, blood_glucose_mgdl, and LDL_mgdl.

# Your code here
clinical <- health %>% 
select(sample_id, sex, blood_glucose_mgdl, LDL_mgdl)
head(clinical)

2.2 From the original health tibble, filter to keep only Female samples whose blood_glucose_mgdl is greater than 100 mg/dL (pre-diabetic range). How many samples meet this criterion?

# Your code here
female_prediabetic <- health %>% 
filter(sex == "Female", blood_glucose_mgdl > 100)
head(female_prediabetic)
nrow(female_prediabetic)
[1] 35

2.3 Filter health to keep only samples with brown hair or blue eyes. Store the result as brown_or_blue.

# Your code here
brown_or_blue <- health %>%
filter(eye_color =="Blue" | hair_color == "Brown")
head(brown_or_blue)
nrow(brown_or_blue)
[1] 116

Part 3 — Creating new variables (mutate)

3.1 Add a column called bmi (Body Mass Index) to health using the formula:

\[BMI = \frac{weight\_kg}{(height\_cm / 100)^2}\]

Round to two decimal places. Save the result back to health.

# Your code here
health <- health %>%
  mutate(bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2, 2))

head(health)
NA

3.2 Add a column called glucose_category that classifies each sample:

  • "Normal" if blood_glucose_mgdl < 100
  • "Pre-diabetic" if between 100 and 125 (inclusive)
  • "Diabetic" if blood_glucose_mgdl > 125

Hint: Use case_when() inside mutate().

# Your code here
health <- health %>%
  mutate(glucose_category = case_when(
    blood_glucose_mgdl < 100 ~ "Normal",
    blood_glucose_mgdl >= 100 & blood_glucose_mgdl <= 125 ~ "Pre-diabetic",
    blood_glucose_mgdl > 125 ~ "Diabetic"
  ))

head(health)
NA

Part 4 — Summarizing by group (group_by, summarize)

4.1 Calculate the mean and standard deviation of bmi separately for Males and Females. Your output should have three columns: sex, mean_bmi, and sd_bmi.

# Your code here
health %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(bmi),
    sd_bmi = sd(bmi)
  )
NA

4.2 Count how many samples fall into each glucose_category, broken down by sex. Your output should have columns sex, glucose_category, and n.

# Your code here
health %>%
  group_by(sex, glucose_category) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

4.3 For each hair_color, calculate the mean LDL_mgdl. Arrange the result from highest to lowest mean LDL.

# Your code here
health %>%
  group_by(hair_color) %>%
  summarise(mean_LDL = mean(LDL_mgdl)) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_LDL))

Part 5 — Visualization with ggplot2

For each plot, make sure to add informative axis labels and a title using labs().

5.1 Histogram — distribution of blood glucose

Plot a histogram of blood_glucose_mgdl. Color the bars by sex using fill. Use alpha = 0.6 so overlapping bars are visible. Set appropriate binwidth.

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = blood_glucose_mgdl, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Blood Glucose Levels",
    x = "Blood Glucose (mg/dL)",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

5.2 Scatter plot — height vs. weight

Create a scatter plot of height_cm (x-axis) vs. weight_kg (y-axis), coloring points by sex. Add a linear regression line for each sex using geom_smooth(method = "lm").

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = height_cm, y = weight_kg, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title = "Height vs Weight by Sex",
    x = "Height (cm)",
    y = "Weight (kg)",
    color = "Sex"
  )

5.3 Box plot — BMI by sex

Make a box plot of bmi for each sex. Overlay the individual data points using geom_jitter() with width = 0.2 and alpha = 0.4.

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = sex, y = bmi)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "BMI by Sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "BMI"
  )

5.4 Bar chart — sample counts by hair color and sex

Using geom_bar(), create a bar chart showing the number of samples for each hair_color, filled by sex. Use position = "dodge" so the bars for each sex are side by side.

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = hair_color, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Sample Counts by Hair Color and Sex",
    x = "Hair Color",
    y = "Number of Samples",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

5.5 Scatter plot — BMI vs. LDL

Plot bmi (x) vs. LDL_mgdl (y), coloring points by glucose_category. Choose a colorblind-friendly palette with scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2"). Does there appear to be a relationship?

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = bmi, y = LDL_mgdl, color = glucose_category)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "BMI vs LDL Cholesterol by Glucose Category",
    x = "BMI",
    y = "LDL Cholesterol (mg/dL)",
    color = "Glucose Category"
  )

5.6 Faceted plot — glucose vs. LDL by sex

Plot blood_glucose_mgdl (x) vs. LDL_mgdl (y) as a scatter plot, then use facet_wrap(~ sex) to create separate panels for Males and Females.

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = blood_glucose_mgdl, y = LDL_mgdl)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(
    title = "Blood Glucose vs LDL Cholesterol by Sex",
    x = "Blood Glucose (mg/dL)",
    y = "LDL Cholesterol (mg/dL)"
  )

Part 6 — Putting it together (open-ended)

6.1 Using any combination of dplyr and ggplot2, create one additional plot of your choice that reveals something interesting about this dataset. Write 2–3 sentences below your plot describing what you observe.

# Your code here
ggplot(health, aes(x = glucose_category, y = bmi, fill = glucose_category)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "BMI by Glucose Category",
    x = "Glucose Category",
    y = "BMI"
  )

Your observations: BMI seems to be higher in Pre-diabetic and Diabetic groups than in the Normal group. This seems to show that individuals with high blood glucose levels also have higher body mass index values. There is extensive overlap among the groups, indicating that BMI does not completely explain glucose levels —
